title: Former New London Hospital Medical Chief Gets Prison for Signing Medicare Brace Orders for Patients He Never Examined
text:
Former New London Hospital Medical Chief Gets Prison for Signing Medicare Brace Orders for Patients He Never Examined
A former chief medical officer at New London Hospital in New Hampshire has been sentenced to one year and one day in federal prison for signing orders for medical braces for Medicare patients he never examined, NHPR reported. Prosecutors had asked for 18 months.
Dr. Steven Powell, 56, pleaded guilty to health care fraud in April 2023. U.S. District Judge Paul Barbadoro sentenced him on October 13, and he must report to prison on November 13. Under his plea agreement, he must repay $761,202.75 to Medicare.
The case is a reminder for older adults and caregivers, whose Medicare numbers make these schemes work. Unneeded braces billed in a patient's name can make it harder to get a brace that patient truly needs later.
Inside the Brace-Ordering Scheme
Between December 2018 and March 2019, Powell signed orders for more than 500 Medicare beneficiaries, according to court documents described by NHPR. About 1,400 claims totaling $1,908,702 were billed, and Medicare paid $761,202. Powell committed the fraud after resigning as the hospital's chief medical officer.
He was paid $15 per consult to sign orders falsely stating he had assessed or treated patients. The orders covered knee, wrist, back, and shoulder braces. He ordered two or more braces for nearly every patient and four or more for at least 71 beneficiaries.
Powell was sentenced for defrauding Medicare by prescribing equipment "without ever seeing, speaking to, or otherwise examining patients," according to the HHS Office of Inspector General.
Court records show how fast the signing went. In one December 2018 packet of 105 pages requiring 75 signatures, Powell completed every signature in 1 minute and 20 seconds. That packet included orders for four braces for a 77-year-old beneficiary who was immobile in the last year of his life and had never met Powell.
FBI Boston Division Special Agent in Charge Ted Docks said Powell had "abandoned all pretense of professional ethics," according to the Justice Department's announcement.
Behind the Telemedicine Middleman
The orders came through a telemedicine company called Expansion. It generated fabricated medical records, routed them to Powell through DocuSign, and sold the signed orders to medical equipment suppliers that billed Medicare. The company's owner, Steven Richardson, was sentenced in August to two years in federal prison in a $110 million telemedicine fraud scheme.
This is a common pattern in medical equipment fraud. Marketers gather Medicare numbers through calls or ads, a paid clinician signs orders without a real visit, and a supplier bills for braces that were never medically needed.
Prosecutors argued Powell's conduct showed calculated decisions that put personal financial gain ahead of his legal duties and patient welfare. The defense did not file a sentencing memorandum, and neither Powell nor his attorney could be reached for comment, NHPR reported.
The charge carried a maximum penalty of 10 years. The judge recommended that Powell serve his time at the lowest custody level possible and as close as possible to his family. The extra day on his sentence makes him eligible for federal good-conduct credit, which can shorten time served.
The FBI and HHS-OIG led the investigation. Sentencing was delayed repeatedly after his 2023 plea because of attorney scheduling conflicts and a medical procedure. Powell, who completed his residency at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center and worked at New London Hospital for 15 years, now lives in Georgia.
Protecting Medicare Accounts From Brace Scams
The HHS Office of Inspector General warns in its nationwide brace scam alert that scammers call Medicare beneficiaries or run ads offering braces described as free and covered by Medicare. Once a person provides or confirms their Medicare information, braces may arrive even if they were never requested.
The agency's advice is blunt: if someone calls offering a free brace billed to Medicare, "hang up immediately." Refuse deliveries of equipment your own doctor did not order, or send them back and note the sender's name and the date. Do not share a Medicare number with anyone other than your own physician's office.
Caregivers can help older relatives review their Medicare Summary Notices or online account statements for equipment, tests, or visits they do not recognize. Unfamiliar charges are worth reporting even if the patient owes nothing.
Suspected fraud can be reported to the HHS-OIG Hotline at 1-800-447-8477 or through the OIG's online fraud reporting page.
Patients who genuinely need a brace should get it through a clinician they know and trust who has examined them. That protects both their health and their future Medicare coverage.
This case is closed, but brace scams remain active. A quick check of each Medicare statement is one of the simplest ways families can protect an older relative.
Key Questions Answered
What was the doctor sentenced for? Health care fraud for signing Medicare brace orders for more than 500 patients he never examined.
What was the sentence? One year and one day in federal prison, plus $761,202.75 in restitution. Prosecutors had sought 18 months.
How do brace scams work? Marketers collect Medicare numbers, paid clinicians sign orders without exams, and suppliers bill Medicare for unneeded braces.
Can a brace scam affect my own care? Yes. If unneeded braces are billed in your name, Medicare may deny a brace you need in the future.
What should I do if a brace arrives that I did not order? Refuse or return it, record the sender and date, and report it to the HHS-OIG Hotline.
How do I report suspected Medicare fraud? Call 1-800-447-8477 or use the OIG's online fraud reporting page.
Published by Medicaldaily.com
